Asset Allocation Strategies

Illustration of portfolio weights, not a recommended allocation.

Asset allocation describes how value is divided among exposures. Its effect depends on holdings, correlations and the period examined; it does not guarantee performance or universally outrank every other decision.

100%
Total Weight in a Normalized Allocation

The selected weights, including cash, should sum to 100%. This is an accounting identity, not evidence that an allocation determines a fixed share of returns.

Three hypothetical allocations

Compare the following invented weights. None is a suitability assessment or a recommended allocation.

💡
Example

Hypothetical A: 80% stock exposures, 15% crypto and 5% cash. Weights total 100%; this is not an age-based recommendation and losses can be permanent.

💡
Example

Hypothetical B: 60% stock exposures, 30% cash and 10% another practice asset. The example does not certify a balanced or suitable real portfolio.

💡
Example

Hypothetical C: 40% stock exposures and 60% cash. This illustrates a different weighting rather than promising capital preservation or retirement income.

Age alone cannot determine a suitable allocation. Objectives, liabilities, time horizon and ability to bear loss also matter; a simulator cannot make that determination.

The 100-Minus-Age Rule

The 100-minus-age shortcut is a simplified heuristic, not a suitability assessment:

Subtract your age from 100 = % in stocks
Age 25: 75% stocks, 25% bonds/cash
Age 50: 50% stocks, 50% bonds/cash
Age 70: 30% stocks, 70% bonds/cash
This shortcut ignores liabilities, product risks and ability to bear losses; it cannot establish suitability.
Pro Tip

Compare hypothetical annual review and threshold rules under the same assumptions. Five-percent drift is an example setting, not a universally appropriate rebalancing trigger.
